summary: Creates a registry for CoRE target attributes, the names that Web Links can carry in discovery protocols like the CoAP link format and Resource Directory. It informs implementers about attribute names and their meanings.

eli5.summary: A list of labels that devices can put on links, to help others figure out what is behind them.

subtitle: A registry for names that describe links in constrained IoT systems.

tldr.problem: CoRE (Constrained RESTful Environments) discovery protocols use Web Linking with target attributes to describe resources, but different systems were choosing different attribute names, risking conflicts and incompatibilities.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9423 creates an IANA registry for target attribute names used in CoRE with an Expert Review policy, ensuring that attributes are named consistently and coordinated across specifications. It seeds the registry with common attributes from CoAP, the Resource Directory, and Web Linking.
tldr.outcome: Systems implementing CoRE can register their attribute names, avoiding future collisions and making discovery more reliable and interoperable.

today: RFC 9423 is an Informational document that created the Target Attributes registry at IANA in April 2024. The registry remains open for new registrations under Expert Review policy, coordinating attribute names for CoRE-based discovery protocols.

sections.title: Web Linking in CoRE
sections.content:
Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) applies web technologies to resource-constrained systems. One key technology is Web Linking (RFC 8288), which CoRE specifications use as the foundation for discovery protocols such as the Link Format used in the Constrained Application Protocol's (CoAP) resource discovery process and the Resource Directory (RD).

Web Links can carry target attributes—names that describe properties of the linked resource, such as its resource type (rt), interface description (if), content format (ct), or maximum size (sz). The Web Linking specification itself does not coordinate the names of target attributes, leaving implementers free to define their own but at the risk of creating conflicts when different systems choose the same name for different purposes.
sections.eli5: When a tiny device (like a sensor) tells other devices what it is, it uses special labels. This RFC creates a list of approved labels so everyone uses the same ones.

sections.title: Why a Registry is Needed
sections.content:
The CoRE Working Group has been discussing setting up a registry for target attribute names since the work on CoRE Link Format (RFC 6690). The update of Web Linking to RFC 8288 provided the formal setting and acknowledgment that while Web Linking does not coordinate attribute names, individual serializations (like CoRE's) should do so.

Without a registry, an unregistered attribute name might be registered later with a different meaning, causing incompatibilities. By creating a registry now, systems implementing CoRE can register their attribute names, ensuring that each name has a consistent meaning across all CoRE-based protocols and implementations. The registry also guides developers toward reasonably short names (important for conserving resources in constrained systems) while preserving very short names for attributes that are likely to be widely used.
sections.eli5: Different groups might invent their own labels without knowing what others chose. A central list prevents confusion and helps new devices pick good names that everyone agrees on.

sections.title: How the Registry Works
sections.content:
RFC 9423 creates a new "Target Attributes" registry under the Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) Parameters registry group at IANA. The registry uses an "Expert Review" policy, meaning that each new registration is reviewed by a designated expert who guides registrants toward appropriate names and ensures quality specifications.

Each registry entry must include an attribute name (lowercase ASCII starting with a letter, with optional digits and hyphens), a brief description, a change controller, and a reference document describing the attribute and its semantics. The expert is instructed to encourage reasonably short names and to direct registrants to provide full specifications—though exceptions can be made when a specification is not available yet but is likely forthcoming.
sections.eli5: When someone wants to register a label, they describe it and an expert checks that it makes sense, does not conflict with other labels, and is documented well.

sections.title: Initial Attributes
sections.content:
The registry is seeded with initial entries from existing CoRE and Web Linking standards. Entries from RFC 6690 (CoRE Link Format) include rt (resource type), if (interface description), sz (maximum size estimate), and ct (Content-Format hint). Additional entries come from CoAP specifications: obs (observable resource), hct (HTTP-CoAP URI mapping), and osc (OSCORE-only hint).

From the Resource Directory (RFC 9176) come ep (Endpoint Name), d (Sector), base (Registration Base URI), and et (Endpoint Type). From Web Linking (RFC 8288) come hreflang, media, title, and type. Certain names like href, anchor, rel, and rev are reserved as not useful for target attributes.
sections.eli5: The list starts with labels that CoRE systems already use, like rt for what kind of resource it is, and if for how to talk to it.

sections.title: Coordination with Related Registries
sections.content: RFC 9423 updates the "RD Parameters" IANA registry created by RFC 9176 to coordinate with the new Target Attributes registry. The RD Parameters registry marks certain entries with an "A" flag, indicating they are target attributes. Per this document, all entries with the "A" flag, including new ones, must also be registered in the Target Attributes registry. This ensures a single source of truth for attribute definitions across CoRE specifications.
sections.eli5: The Resource Directory has its own list of labels. This RFC makes sure that any label used in both places is defined in the same central registry.
